rule: adjusted_score desc, total_score desc; dedupe by arXiv id / URL / id / title

papers.title: Generative Search and Recommendation at Shopify
papers.authors: Juhana Kangaspunta, Khalil Hajji, Darshan Fofadiya, Kyumin Park, Michael Garner, Anthony Maltsev, Ryan Synk, Jose Sepulv...
papers.summary: Search and recommendation at Shopify have to retrieve relevant products from a changing catalog of billions of items under tight latency limits. This report casts both tasks as generating semantic IDs: short sequences of content-derived tokens that represent products. The model is jointly pretrained on catalog and behavioral data so search and recommendation share a representation and a training objective. Reinforcement learning further improves judged search relevance, and distillation from task-specific experts improves recommendation without a statistically detected loss in search quality. In an online test on the home recommendation feed, adding the model raised attributed orders by 7.95%, converting users by 8.60%, and conversion rate by 9.85% on that feed.

papers.title: RedMall: Generative Recommendation for Large-Scale E-commerce
papers.authors: Kunyang Zhou, Xin Jia, Yi Yang, Yongjun Yang, Manjie Xu, Honglei Zhang, Yan Zhu, Kai Zuo, Xu Tang, Zheng Wang
papers.summary: Generative retrieval outputs a Semantic ID (SID), but several products can share one SID, and which of them are finally retrieved directly affects online gains. RedMall is a generative model for e-commerce recommendation and ad retrieval. Besides changes to the architecture and training objectives, such as treating items that were shown but not clicked as negatives, it handles this step explicitly. In serving, each product under the same SID gets a score, a weighted mix of the GMV it brought per thousand impressions in the past, weighted most, and its orders per thousand impressions, and only the top-scoring ones are kept. In the e-commerce recommendation A/B test, the full model raised GMV by 1.08%. The authors also tested this step on its own in ad retrieval: without it, the online lift in ad retrieval is no longer significant, because duplicates are filtered downstream and only about half as many items get through. ==How a SID is turned into products also decides how much generative retrieval gains==.

papers.title: TS-GEAR: Taobao Shangou GEnerative Ad Retrieval
papers.authors: Guofeng Tong, Xu Zhang, Guangliang Yu, Haiqiang Wang, Guannan Cong, Xing Guo, Yang Zhou, Jingjing Duan, Shuang Li, Feng ...
papers.summary: In food delivery search, a merchant that cannot deliver to the user is an invalid candidate, yet common SIDs encode only content, so such merchants are filtered after generation and waste beam slots. TS-GEAR from Taobao Shangou writes location into the ID: the first three tokens come from a geographic grid code, the last three carry content, and decoding restricts the first two tokens to the user's cell and its eight neighbors. At the production retrieval radius, 95.8% of its top 50 candidates are deliverable, while the strongest baseline, OneLoc, manages only a little over a third. The paper's explanation is that ==once location is generated end to end, the model learns how to order merchants within reach==, whereas a post-hoc filter can only delete bad ones. In an online A/B test, ad revenue rose 4.2%.

papers.title: Not All Branches Are Equal: Adaptive Semantic ID Construction for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Guy Hadad, Haggai Roitman, Bracha Shapira
papers.summary: Generative recommendation often assumes that each token of a SID carries its own independent meaning. The authors checked RQ-VAE IDs on Amazon Beauty: two products sharing only the first token have a mean cosine similarity of 0.740, while two sharing only the last three tokens reach just 0.582, about the same as a random pair. ==Later tokens have no stable meaning apart from their prefix==, so a SID is really a path in a tree. AST therefore builds the tree directly by clustering product embeddings from the top down, with each node choosing its number of branches by cluster quality. On five Amazon datasets it beats the strongest baseline by 13.08% on average, and because the methods share embeddings and the generative model, the gap comes only from how the IDs are built.

papers.title: Rethinking Latent Reasoning for Generative Recommendation: Beyond Teacher-Generated CoT and Recurrent Hidden-State Feedback
papers.authors: Yiwen Chen, Fuwei Zhang, Zehao Chen, Deqing Wang, Hehan Li, Peizhi Xu, Hanmeng Liu, Shuanglong Li, Xin Pei, Fuzhen Zhuan...
papers.summary: Latent reasoning for generative recommendation usually needs a teacher model to write chain-of-thought traces, which is costly and hard to stabilize. This paper skips teacher generation. It builds semantic targets from the text meaning of items already in a user's history, and uses those targets to supervise the model's intermediate tokens that are reserved for reasoning steps, without looking at the next-item label. With supervised fine-tuning alone, the method outperforms the compared baselines across four recommendation benchmarks. On Beauty, it improves NDCG@1 by 20.6% and NDCG@5 by 10.3% over MiniOneRec. Controlled ablations indicate that the gain comes from input-matched historical semantic supervision, not from extra tokens by themselves.

papers.title: IntentLens: Grounding Underspecified Multimodal Queries for Recommendation via Tool-Augmented Reasoning
papers.authors: Xiao Chen, Dong Fang, Haitao Li, Qing Li
papers.summary: A user points a camera at a cafe dish and asks for something with this kind of vibe, but more affordable and better for a quick lunch nearby. Style and budget stay unstated, so direct similarity between query and candidates easily ranks the wrong places first. IntentLens adds a step before ranking: a multimodal LLM calls tools that inspect the image and search the user's history, then rewrites the vague request as an explicit text query. Candidates are enriched with details such as reviews and price before a lightweight two-tower model scores them. On the Google review data, holding the two-tower model and candidates fixed and changing only the query raises MRR from 33.6% to 40.2%, and the annotated reference query reaches 44.4%. These queries are synthesized by LLMs, and each request takes several seconds.

papers.title: RecGroupMemory: Feedback-Aware Cohort Memory for E-Commerce Recommendation
papers.authors: Wendong Zhang, Weipeng Huang, Zhixin Ma, Bin Zhang, Dimin Wang
papers.summary: When a large model plans a recommendation workflow, it can be given memory of how a group of users has behaved. The difficulty is that new transaction feedback arrives the next day and the advice should change, while the record of the group definition, the observation window and the statistics must not be rewritten along the way. RecGroupMemory splits the memory in two layers. One is a read-only record of observations and the other is a profile with advice. The previous day's feedback may change only the second layer, and a check confirms the observations are unchanged, otherwise the original record is kept. In online comparisons on low-purchasing-power users chosen by the business team at an e-commerce platform, the group using memory alone had 1.58% more transacting users than its no-memory baseline. The group that added feedback revision had 1.78% more than its own no-memory baseline.

papers.title: LEGIT: Live Eligibility Gating over Identifier Tries for Constrained Decoding of Heterogeneous Pages
papers.authors: Felix Fang, Zheng Liu, Robert Saliba
papers.summary: Uber Eats generative search writes a whole page of stores and menu items in one decode, and every token must keep each store real, deliverable and unrepeated, with each item belonging to the store above it. The authors compared 36 implementations: the direct GPU version makes each token about 5 times as slow as unconstrained decoding, while the GPU compute units are active at most 5.42% of the time. Hardware counters and ablations both point to kernel launches and CPU waits on the GPU as the overhead. ==The arithmetic of the constraint is light, and the expense is the round trip to the GPU for each group of sequences==. Walking the trie on the CPU while the model runs its forward pass brings the cost down to about 1.7 times, with no custom kernel.

papers.title: RoutingTrie: Metadata Routing for Constrained Generative Retrieval
papers.authors: Darshan Fofadiya, Yang Liu, Shuying Sun, Kyumin Park, Juhana Kangaspunta
papers.summary: Generative retrieval often has to honor a condition, such as returning only products from one shop. The usual approach filters after generation, but by then the beam is full of other shops' candidates and few results survive. RoutingTrie moves the filter ahead of beam selection at every step: each edge of the SID trie records which shops, countries and other values occur below it, and decoding first blocks branches that cannot reach the requested value. Fields with few values are stored as bitmaps and fields with huge value sets, such as shop ID, as sorted lists. Replaying historical purchases through a production system with a shop filter raises Hit@100 from 67.5% to 96.1% and adds only 1.1 ms of request latency. ==The model scores are unchanged, so the gain comes from no longer wasting the beam==.

papers.title: CascadeRec: Deployed Adaptive LLM Compute Allocation for Multi-Tenant Content Recommendation
papers.authors: Kai Zhao, Guilin Zhang, Xiang Cheng, Xiquan Cui, Henry Heng, Xu Chu, Alet Blanken
papers.summary: Large language models are attractive rerankers, but running an expensive model on every request is costly and often hurts users with short histories. This production system, deployed for content recommendation at a large financial-planning software provider, reranks every request with a lightweight first tier. A router then uses segment cues such as history length to escalate only the requests more likely to benefit to a more expensive second tier, such as a larger model or multi-path reasoning. In a production experiment lasting over a month, it cut inference cost by about 10% versus using the expensive tier uniformly, with little latency impact and no observed quality regression. On MovieLens-1M and Amazon Electronics, uniform LLM reranking lowers NDCG@10 for sparse-history users by up to 30%, and the only statistically significant gain appears among users with the longest histories.

papers.title: STCRank: Spatio-temporal Collaborative Ranking for Interactive Recommender System at Kuaishou E-shop
papers.authors: Boyang Xia, Ruilin Bao, Hanjun Jiang, Jun Wang, Wenwu Ou
papers.summary: In a full-screen e-commerce feed where each swipe down brings the next item, the two ranking objectives of whether the user buys and whether they keep swiping fight each other. Kuaishou E-shop's data show that after a purchase, users leave right away without swiping 61.3% of the time. With the usual labels, every one of those purchases becomes a negative sample for the swipe objective, so the learned swipe score ends up pushing down the items that sell. The authors drop purchase-then-exit samples from the swipe negatives. Ranking also stops picking the top-scoring item one screen at a time. Instead it scores different orderings of the next few items: each item's value is multiplied by the probability that the user swipes far enough to reach it, and the ordering with the highest total wins. Adding this look-ahead ranking to the full-screen feed alone raised online purchases by 2.10%. Teams running immersive feeds should check their objectives for conflicting labels first.

papers.title: SepLRM: A Foundation Model Paradigm for Recommendation
papers.authors: Di Chen, Xijun Xiao, Qin Ren, Weijiang Lai, Zhijian Pan, Zhentao Pan, Pengfei Nie, Cheng Yuan, Zixuan Tan, Xuyang Liu, T...
papers.summary: Models for different recommendation stages and business lines each encode the same long user history, and this repeated cost gets harder to justify as sequences grow. SepLRM pulls that step out: one shared foundation model runs the encoder and stores its final-layer representation of every behavior as a KV cache, and each downstream model builds queries from its own candidates and context and reads the cache with cross-attention. Because the cut sits between encoder and decoder, downstream computation matches the end-to-end model, and without compression about 100% of the AUC gain from long sequences is preserved. ==A high AUC on the foundation model does not mean its exported cache is useful==, since encoder-only and decoder-only versions keep nearly the same AUC while downstream retention falls to around ninety percent. Online, in advertising and e-commerce, ROI reaches 8.62 times and 2.62 times that of matched end-to-end models.

papers.title: Proactive Dimension-Adaptive Denoising for Graph Collaborative Filtering via Representation Coherence
papers.authors: Wenjun Li, Dong Zhao, Jiaying Shi, Juan Zhang, Zhaoming Pan, Zhimin Zhang
papers.summary: Denoising for implicit feedback almost always uses training loss to decide which interactions are noise, but loss only grows after the model has been misled, and it is also disturbed by negative sampling and training stage. NDL from NetEase adds a new signal: the cosine similarity between an interaction's representation and the mean representation of that user's past interactions, where larger deviation means more suspicion, and ==this signal is available before the model makes a prediction error==. Active users rely mainly on this signal, while cold-start users fall back to training loss. The fused suspicion score decides how many embedding dimensions an interaction may use, with more suspicious interactions getting fewer. On public datasets where ratings below three count as noise, Recall@5 beats the strongest baseline DAR by 5.63% to 17.95%, with larger gains on sparser data. The change lives only in training and serving keeps LightGCN embeddings of the same shape, although the method has not yet been deployed online.

papers.title: OptiCover: A Scalable and Multi-Surface Framework for Cold-Start Visual Optimization under Semantic Constraints
papers.authors: Guillaume Guy, Mihajlo Grbovic, Joe Mills, Selen Uguroglu, Liwei He, Pratiksha Kadam, Nalini Kartha, Qian Aria Li
papers.summary: Airbnb wants to choose cover photos for hosts, but over 90% of listing photos have never been a cover and so have no click data to learn from. The authors first screen candidates with indirect cues, use a VLM to check that a photo truly represents the listing, and then pick by predicted CTR, which raises CTR by 1.5% in a HomePage A/B test. The most interesting part is a pair of experiments on Search. Picking the photo with the highest predicted clicks raises CTR significantly but leaves bookers without a significant change, and analysis shows the extra clicks mainly move bookings from one listing to another. Narrowing candidates by the guest's filter, such as pools, before choosing leaves CTR without a significant change but raises bookers significantly by 0.35%. ==On Search, narrowing candidates by guest intent brings more bookings than pushing up clicks==.

papers.title: SAGE-PAIR: Source-Pretrained Routed Residual Adaptation for Sparse-Feedback Recommendation
papers.authors: Weiqing Zeng, Zida Yang, Guquan You, Jiexin Zheng, Cong Wang
papers.summary: When a recommender moves into a new serving window, the target window often has too little feedback to retrain the live model. This paper freezes the original model and adds only a residual: the item features are click and like rates in the source window (exactly two dimensions), and the expert basis is a small set of anchors in that same plane. A soft router weights those anchors from the user's source-window behavior profile, and the extra term added to the original score is the inner product of the item features with that mixed direction. Scarce target feedback only updates these residual parameters. On a locked KuaiSAR-v2 test split, the full method raises NDCG@10 by 1.77% relative. Adding the routed experts gives a further 0.25% relative gain over source-pretrained residual adaptation without routing. When feedback is sparse, whether an update direction can be estimated may matter more than how many labels there are.

papers.title: Query- and Candidate-Aware Long User Sequence Modeling for Sponsored Product Ranking in Search
papers.authors: Dongyue Xie, Sergey Kolbin, Manavender Malgireddy, Iurii Shcherbak, Weixing Tang, Arushi Jain, Wanchen Shao, Kurt Zimmer...
papers.summary: When sponsored search ranking uses long-term behavior, the usual approach searches history for actions similar to the candidate product, yet the current query also indicates which history matters. Beyond recent behavior, Wayfair retrieves one batch of long-term actions by candidate and another by query, then feeds them to a Transformer with two context tokens for the query and the candidate. Offline, the two retrieval channels together give a larger AUC gain than either alone, which suggests the history they find is complementary. Another finding is that injecting the candidate into every history token cannot be skipped, since removing it makes the model clearly worse than the production baseline, and ==a single global candidate token with indirect interaction cannot make up for it==. In an online A/B test of the full model, CTR rose 6.0%, orders per impression rose 11.5%, and model serving latency increased by about 12%.

papers.title: Slim Foundation Models for Latency-Critical Recommendation Serving
papers.authors: Danyal Aftab, Anas Zafar, Assadig Abakr, Steven Davy
papers.summary: Putting an LLM in the online CTR path is too expensive, so existing methods mostly compute LLM outputs offline and store them, and must regenerate them whenever the item or feature catalog changes. SlimFM tries to run the LLM directly online, first applying structured pruning to LLaMA3 to remove 44% of the parameters. LoRA fine-tuning then makes the model produce one embedding per feature field, such as MovieID, and similarity between fields reweights the feature interactions of the CTR model. On FM, the pruned model keeps 99.77% of the full model's mean AUC, and inference is up to 3.4 times faster than with existing LLM-enhanced methods. It holds no clear accuracy lead, reaching the highest AUC among the LLM-enhanced methods in fewer than half of the model and dataset combinations, so ==its main value lies in latency==.

papers.title: CHO-Bench: How Do Context Hints Affect Ad Rankings in LLM Advertising?
papers.authors: Shiqi Zhang, Yang Fei, Xiaokui Xiao
papers.summary: ChatGPT Ads lets advertisers write natural-language hints about what a product is, who it suits, and when it helps, and these hints feed ad ranking separately from the ad card shown to users. How should such hints be written? The authors split them into seven styles from marketing frameworks, add one that mixes all seven, and run over 1.19 million paired comparisons with and without hints. Adding hints moves an ad up by 0.56 to 1.16 positions on average, but the seven styles differ little and the mix has no consistent advantage. Measured by rank gain, the difference shows up in the ranker: embedding rankers favor hints about usage situations, while LLM rankers favor hints about target audiences. Adding more hints generally improves rank further, with diminishing marginal gains. In these experiments only the evaluated ad receives hints and the rankers are offline, so the effect when competitors also write hints remains a separate question.

papers.title: Not Your Diary, Just Your Topic: Grading the Wrong-User Control
papers.authors: Karina Romanova, Igor Kiselev, Vladimir Platonov, Viliana Devbunova, Gregory Leleytner, Adeliya Leleytner, Lina Veltman,...
papers.summary: A common personalization check replaces a user's own history with someone else's and watches accuracy drop. That swap also changes the topics in the history, so the drop may not mean the system recognized the person. On a frozen language model and LaMP-2 news classification, a user's own history beats using no history by 2.3 points. Keeping only each article's category label and dropping the text already reproduces 86% of the gap between own history and a random user's history. Synthetic histories are stitched from other users' articles that are closest in text to the target profile. When each slot must also match the category label at the same position in the original history, a user's own history beats this synthetic history by only 0.9 points. On unseen users, a user's own history beats similar-user histories by only 0.65 points, which is not yet strong evidence. Personalization tests should look at unseen users and compare against content-matched histories.

papers.title: Not Yet in the Profile: Uncertainty-Aware Dynamic User Profiling by Learning from Future Interactions
papers.authors: Jieyong Kim, Neil Shah, Dong Wang
papers.summary: When an LLM maintains a user profile, new behavior often has several readings: a fantasy fan rating a fantasy drawing guide 3 out of 5 may be tiring of fantasy, or may simply dislike drawing guides. Existing methods must either write it into the profile at once or discard it, and a wrong entry keeps misleading later predictions. UAPM adds two stores outside the profile that the downstream model cannot read, one holding unresolved readings with their evidence and one recording what evidence this user needs before a conclusion. In training, a Teacher that sees the user's future behavior guides each decision of a Student, and at deployment the Student uses only current information. Under the same profile length, it beats the best baseline by up to 5%, and removing either store worsens almost every metric. ==Held entries rarely move straight into the profile and mainly serve as evidence for later profile edits==.

papers.title: Beyond Ranking: Are Decision Models Calibrated Relevance Scorers?
papers.authors: Shengyao Zhuang, Xueguang Ma, Matthias Petri, Jimmy Lin
papers.summary: Decision models such as Jev output a probability for each relevance level directly, and the vendor promises those probabilities are calibrated. Checked against TREC human judgments, only 66% of the documents it scores above 0.9 are actually relevant, and none of the other models tested is calibrated either. The error is mostly one of scale, so a two-parameter Platt calibration fitted on one year of labels corrects much of it on a new year and a new corpus. With calibrated probabilities, choosing how many documents to keep per query by expected F1 needs no tuned threshold, matches a threshold tuned for the job, and clearly beats a fixed top-ten cut. ==Ranking well does not mean the probabilities are right==, so anyone truncating RAG context by probability needs at least one set of their own human labels to calibrate against.

papers.title: Yuanbao-Reranker: Document-Grounded Synthesis and Preference Distillation for Text Reranking
papers.authors: Hongyuan Xu, Dezhi Ye, Jiahao Cao, Jie Liu, Haijin Liang, Haibo Shi, Jin Ma
papers.summary: Rerankers fine-tuned pointwise on relevant and not-relevant labels have a gap: every negative carries the same label, so the model never learns which negatives sit closer to the positive. Tencent's Yuanbao Search pairs each positive with three negatives of different difficulty and adds a distillation loss that treats the teacher's score gap as a lower bound, so the student stops being penalized once it reaches that distance. On held-out training groups, the share with all three negative tiers ordered correctly rises from 36.4% to 69.7%, while separating positives from negatives was already near perfect. Replacing the lower bound with squared error that chases the gap scores below having no such loss at all. ==The order among negatives is the information binary labels leave out==, and the final 4B student beats the 8B model that taught it on the five-benchmark average.

papers.title: Lightfoot: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Exact, Model-Free Document Deletion
papers.authors: Uday Allu
papers.summary: GraphRAG in production has two costs that papers rarely count: what it takes to build the graph, and how painful it is to delete a document. When a contract expires or a user asks for erasure, entity summaries that blend several documents are hard to take apart. Lightfoot requires every record in the graph to be computed only from single-passage extractions, with one model call per passage, none at retrieval, and deletion as a plain database operation. After deleting 10% of the documents on the full MuSiQue corpus, the graph is identical to a fresh index of the survivors, while LightRAG needs 2,187 model calls and 3.7 hours to delete the same documents. The price is accuracy that trades wins with HippoRAG 2 and falls clearly behind on 2WikiMultiHopQA. ==Exact deletion works because no record comes from a model call that read several passages==.

papers.title: SPARSEUP: Towards Better Recipes for Training Modern Learned Sparse Retrievers
papers.authors: Thibault Formal, Pierre Erbacher, Cosimo Rulli
papers.summary: Sparse retrievers like SPLADE, moved onto newer backbones such as ModernBERT, often train poorly, and RoBERTa does not train at all. The authors trace this to the starting point: most of the new backbones' vocabulary scores are already positive, so at the start of training almost every term is active, the document representation is dense, and the gradient that tells terms apart weakens. The fix has three steps. Before training, one constant is subtracted from all scores, set at a high percentile of the score distribution estimated on a small sample of documents. Each input position may activate at most 12 terms. Case and word-boundary variants of the same word are merged. The final model reaches 56.4 average nDCG@10 on BEIR, only 1.5 points below a dense model trained on the same backbone and data. Anyone moving sparse retrieval to a new backbone can start with these three steps.

papers.title: Calibrating Document-Local Boundaries for Contextual Chunk Retrieval
papers.authors: Yuanxiang Wang, Hui Jiang, Da Zhu, Zhihua Chang
papers.summary: Late Chunking encodes a whole document before splitting it, which preserves context but makes similar chunks of the same document harder to tell apart. On InSeNT, a baseline fine-tuned with same-document negatives, 82.21% of the failed queries have another chunk of the same document scoring above the correct one. DcLBC from Alibaba's Qwen team changes two things. It scales a query's scores up more when the correct chunk leads the highest-scoring wrong chunk of the same document by less, and it tells the attention layers during encoding where the chunk boundaries are. Split into four tiers by same-document competition, the NDCG@10 gain concentrates in the hardest tier at 5.46 points, while the two easiest tiers barely move. ==Many long-document retrieval errors come from telling apart chunks of the same document==.

papers.title: CoRA-Bench: Evaluating Evidence Preservation by Context Selectors Under Token Budgets
papers.authors: Huzaifa Pardawala, Siddhant Sukhani, Sudheer Chava, Agam Shah
papers.summary: Filtering content before long-context inference saves tokens, but it can also throw away the evidence the answer needs. CoRA-Bench compares truncation, BM25, dense retrieval, reranking and two compression methods under the same token budgets, and no method wins everywhere. On NoLiMa, where evidence and question share little wording, dense retrieval reaches 0.908 evidence recall against 0.467 for BM25, and on BABILong, with explicit surface cues, BM25 leads instead. Keeping evidence is not the same as answering correctly either: under verbatim scoring Provence keeps almost no complete evidence on LongMemEval, yet its answer accuracy is 66.60%. ==When choosing a context selector, look at evidence recall and answer accuracy separately==.

papers.title: NIFT-SQL: Customer-Supervised Table Scoring for Enterprise Text-to-SQL Retrieval
papers.authors: Arjun Rao, Nishant Gopinath
papers.summary: The first step of enterprise text-to-SQL is finding the tables, yet schemas often offer only cryptic table and column names. NIFT-SQL trains separately on each customer's example questions, has a small cross-encoder judge for every table whether it is needed, and fuses that with hybrid search over a retriever fine-tuned the same way. On LiveSQLBench-Large, with nearly a thousand tables, the share of questions with every needed table in the top fifteen is 21.8% for hybrid search and 85.6% for NIFT-SQL, while the fine-tuned retriever alone reaches 70.4%. The lead is not stable: on a newer BEAVER release, trained only on synthetic questions, it loses to the fine-tuned retriever on real questions. ==With labeled questions in hand, a fine-tuned retriever is itself a cheap and strong baseline==.

papers.title: PatternBloom: Empowering Agentic RAG with Externalized RL-Distilled Graph Patterns
papers.authors: Yi Ge, Heng Huang
papers.summary: RAG agents trained with reinforcement learning can learn to fetch better content, yet the steps for reasoning through a given type of question are worked out from scratch every time. PatternBloom abstracts high-scoring reasoning runs into templates that keep only entity types (the paper calls the store Graph Pattern Memory, and one example goes from a film to its director to the director's nationality). There are 27 such templates, kept outside the model and looked up first so evidence is gathered along them. On MuSiQue questions needing five or more hops, its EM is 17.4, against 3.9 for R1-Searcher, the highest of the compared methods. ==Reasoning paths that recur across multi-hop questions can themselves be the thing you retrieve==. People can read and edit these templates, though all experiments use Wikipedia corpora.

papers.title: Search-by-Answer Bias in Retrieval Models
papers.authors: Adiel Avigad, Shauli Ravfogel, Yoav Goldberg
papers.summary: Dense retrieval should find passages by the relation a query asks about, but this paper shows it leans toward answers the model already knows. The authors build sentence pairs, one kind changing only the answer entity, the other pairing a right-relation sentence holding an alternative answer with a wrong-relation sentence holding the familiar answer. Across eight retrievers, the higher the probability a model gives an answer, the higher it scores passages containing that answer. On examples where the model already favors the canonical answer, Qwen3-Embedding-8B picks the familiar sentence 94.6% of the time when only the answer differs, against 50% with no bias, and ranks the wrong-relation sentence first 65.0% of the time. ==For queries with several valid answers or answers that go stale, retrieval is easily pulled toward what the model remembers==. All test sentences come from templates.

papers.title: TRIAD: Multimodal Retrieval across Abstraction, Constraints, and State
papers.authors: Xiangyang Wu, Chen Ju, Xu Chen, Likang Peng, Jinsong Lan, Haihong Tang, Yang Hu
papers.summary: In multimodal retrieval for agents, top results can look very similar to the request and still fail to satisfy it. TRIAD tests twenty model configurations on three kinds of tasks, hierarchical concepts, positive and negative constraints, and multi-turn dialogue, and no configuration leads on all six subsets. Multi-turn results are the clearest: when the same final request is spread over several turns, mAP falls in 39 of 40 comparisons, and the loss concentrates in sessions where the user revises a condition, such as asking for orange and then changing to blue. Keeping only the last turn does not fix it and is worse overall than keeping the full history. ==Multi-turn retrieval has to keep the conditions still in force and drop the values that were replaced==, and current embedding models generally lose ground at this step.

papers.title: RecoGEM: A Serving System for Production-Scale Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Xiangrui Yang, Yunfeng Zhao, Jiawei Yang, Fangyu Zhang, Enrui Zhao, Liang Zeng, Cheng Peng, Minhui Xie, Jiaqiang Liu, Xi...
papers.summary: Generative recommendation decodes token by token just like an LLM, yet moving an LLM serving stack over works poorly, and this Kuaishou paper on RecoGEM explains why. LLM attention cost sits in long sequences, while each candidate in generative recommendation reads only a few SID tokens, so the cost moves to a huge number of short rows after beam expansion. Every step also has its own vocabulary and tensor shape, and top-k selection becomes heavy work on the critical path. The team hands candidate state between steps and live updates to a separate runtime, and compiles the engine separately for the shape of each step. On the production OneModel workload, one serving instance exceeds 1000 QPS with P99 below 35 ms, and throughput is 2.88 times that of the same system with a uniform shape and ordinary kernels. ==The cost of generative recommendation concentrates in short sequences over large candidate sets, so serving has to be designed around that shape.==

papers.title: Firepool: Brokering Warm GPU Capacity for Agentic and RL Workloads at LinkedIn
papers.authors: Ankit Goyal, Santosh Jha, Zhuo Zhi, Youmin Han, Cong Gu, Chen Xie, Animesh Singh
papers.summary: Agents and RL training issue huge numbers of GPU jobs that run for seconds, yet starting a Pod takes twenty to thirty seconds, and LinkedIn built Firepool to remove that wait. The hard part of a warm pool is that the next job must be able to use an existing Pod, so Pods of one hardware profile share a base image, and code and dependencies are installed only when a job starts. A Pod is reused only for the caller that last used it, and when the caller or session changes, a standby Pod on the same card that holds no GPU memory takes over in under a second. During a sampled production peak, 94.7% of Pod requests were served from warm or standby capacity. Under a two-GPU cap, agent and RL loops finished 13 times and 10.8 times faster than with a new Pod per job. ==The advantage disappears once jobs get long, because only startup time is saved.==

papers.title: Inside the Trap: A Renewal Law for Prefix-Cache Collapse in LLM Agent Serving
papers.authors: Akshat Valse, Ali Jannesari
papers.summary: Multi-turn LLM agents rely on prefix caching to skip repeated work, but this paper finds a trap. After a sudden burst of sessions, an engine can fall into a state where every turn misses the cache and the backlog never drains, even at a load it handled before. In paired tests on two serving engines, two GPUs and two models, a burst of 200 sessions left the engine stuck to the end in all 30 runs, while every matched run without a burst stayed healthy. The authors model the stuck state as a queue in which every turn misses and derive how the backlog grows. The way out is simple: capping the number of concurrent sessions rescues an already trapped engine at the same load. Agent serving has to guard against bursts that wipe out the cache, not just watch average load.

papers.title: Turbocharging PiPNN for Proximity and k-NN Graph Building
papers.authors: Tobias Rubel, Richard Wen, Guy Blelloch, Laxman Dhulipala, Lars Gottesbüren, Jakub Łącki, Vahab Mirrokni
papers.summary: Graph indexes for vector search, such as HNSW and Vamana, answer queries fast but take hours or even days to build on large datasets. PiPNN speeds this up by splitting the vectors into small blocks, finding neighbors inside each block with matrix multiplication, and merging the results into one graph. This paper pushes that route further. It quantizes the vectors to low precision to cut memory traffic, and it fuses the matrix multiplication with picking the top K neighbors, so the full distance matrix is never written back to memory. On CPUs, index building is up to 8 times faster than the original PiPNN. On GPUs it is up to 50 times faster than CAGRA, with query performance at high recall matching or beating the baselines. Teams that rebuild vector indexes often may no longer be held back by build time.

papers.title: e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs)
papers.authors: Swann Bessa, Pierre-Emmanuel Mazaré, Gergely Szilvasy, Hugo Touvron, David Picard, Matthijs Douze, Hervé Jégou
papers.summary: Large-scale embedding clustering still often uses Lloyd's k-means, which takes many epochs and is awkward to tune. This paper turns the updates into mini-batches with an exponential moving average, and it gives scaling rules that set the decay rate and batch size from the number of clusters and the dataset size, so those knobs can be set without a hyperparameter sweep. Across embedding datasets, it reaches the loss of Lloyd k-means at 25 epochs in about two to three epochs, which translates to 10 to 45 times faster GPU wall-clock time than strong existing implementations. As one example, it partitions very large DINO embedding collections into many millions of clusters in just a few epochs, with a loss below Lloyd's longer training run.

papers.title: How We Built TLX: A Hardware-Native GPU Compiler for Production ML at Scale
papers.summary: The performance of recent GPUs depends more and more on how groups of threads divide the work, for example one group moving data while another multiplies matrices. CUDA can express this division but needs large amounts of architecture-specific orchestration code, and Triton hides it inside the compiler. Meta added a layer called TLX on top of Triton, so engineers keep writing Python and spell out thread-group roles and synchronization only where it matters. For recommendation engineers, the most concrete example is user features at scoring time, since the same features are typically copied dozens of times to match the candidates. Meta moved that copy inside the kernel and changed the model along with it, cutting compute-intensive net latency by up to two thirds. Training of the GEM ads model reached 20% to 25% end-to-end MFU on several thousand Blackwell GPUs. ==Kernel optimization is becoming a routine tool for ML engineers.==

papers.title: Detent: Batch-Invariant LLM Serving and RL Rollouts at Near-Stock Speed
papers.authors: Peixu Xin, Runchuan Feng, Jiazhen Guo, Kan Wu, Ming Yin
papers.summary: The same request can produce different output bits just because the other requests in its batch changed. On GSM8K, changing only the load changes the answers of SGLang with standard settings on 33 problems. The root cause is that engines pick kernels from the state of the batch, and two kernels computing the same sum can round it differently. Detent writes the kernel selection logic as a program it can analyze, finds the fewest values that must be fixed, and tunes those values per workload before deployment, keeping all the fast kernels. Once tuned, latency per output token is 1.04 to 1.17 times that of standard settings, while the engines' own deterministic modes cost far more. A trainer using the same kernels and fixed values matches the rollout bit for bit. ==Many fast kernels are unaffected by the batch on their own, so only a few values read during selection need fixing.==

papers.title: FOSCAR: Accelerating Decode Attention over 2- and 4-Bit KV Caches through Affine Folding
papers.authors: Donglin Zhuang, Pragaash Ponnusamy, Xiaoxia Wu, Shuaiwen Leon Song, Zhongzhu Zhou
papers.summary: Decode attention streams the key-value cache for every newly generated token. Packing that cache into low-bit integers reduces memory traffic, but it does not automatically save latency, because converting each value and applying scale and offset before the Tensor Cores saturates instruction-issue throughput. This method leaves those per-value fixes off the cached values. It folds the scale and offset onto the other matrix operand or the product output, depending on the quantization scheme, and preserves the dequantized attention result in exact arithmetic. On H100, the INT2 and INT4 kernels reach geo-mean speedups of 3.36 times and 2.83 times over FlashInfer BF16.

papers.title: ResServe: Accurate and Efficient FP4 LLM Inference with Residue Compensation
papers.authors: Shuo Rong, Ruibo Fan, Jiawen Wen, Xiaowen Chu
papers.summary: Block-scaled 4-bit floating-point inference lowers the cost of large language models but can hurt task quality. Decode matrices are often narrow, which leaves spare hardware capacity. This system keeps an FP4 activation base plus an FP4-quantized residue that represents what quantization discarded, uses the spare capacity to compute the residue on chip, and adds it back without extra result transfers. On NVIDIA B200, the extra request latency is at most 3.4% over uncompensated 4-bit weights and activations, while request latency falls 22.4% to 53.3% relative to 4-bit weights with 8-bit activations. Across five models, code-generation accuracy improves by a mean of 15.04% relative to same-format inference without compensation.

papers.title: Hibana: Fast Agentic Inference on Unified-Memory Devices
papers.authors: Yahya Emara, Chi-Chih Chang, Anthony Fei, Ahmed F. AbouElhamayed, Chong-Yan Chen, Hung-Yueh Chiang, Kai-Chiang Wu, Moham...
papers.summary: Unified-memory devices such as the DGX Spark can hold large models, but memory bandwidth is limited, so decode is often stuck reading weights, and agent session state competes with those weights for the same memory. Hibana changes three things in response: requests in a batch share one set of experts to cut weight reads, inactive session state moves to SSD, and speculative decoding generates several tokens per step with the number adjusted from recent acceptance rates. Replaying recorded agent sessions on one DGX Spark, it completes up to 3.4 times as many tasks per hour as other frameworks, and peak decode throughput at each system's best concurrency reaches up to 3.9 times. The fast profile is lossy, and three-bit weights and relaxed verification cost a few points of accuracy on some tasks. ==Local inference has to save the memory traffic behind each accepted token.==

papers.title: Practice Makes Precise: At CoRL, NVIDIA and Partners Reveal How Robots Rehearse Delicate Work in Simulation
papers.summary: Simulation used to be mostly for teaching robots to walk, and the work NVIDIA showed at CoRL pushes it toward fine jobs like aligning gears and connecting cables. AlphaNIST shows the shift best. A single policy learns every task on the NIST assembly board, handling millimeter-scale parts with nothing but a yes-or-no success signal. Its training success tops 98%, against 81% for separate per-task policies, and it uses roughly 39 times less GPU time. The sampling method behind it is plain: practice concentrates on tasks the policy succeeds at about half the time. ==Training budget should go to what is still unlearned==, the same instinct as training on hard samples in recommendation.

papers.title: RoboColosseum: Evaluating Physical Intelligence at Scale In-The-Wild
papers.authors: Tan Sang Nguyen, Yi Ru Wang, Shailesh Shailesh, Gang Yang, Jiamo Hu, Jianuo Jiang, Haoquan Fang, Zhongzheng Ren, Zhongyi...
papers.summary: Ranking general-purpose robot policies is hard because real-robot experiments are difficult to reproduce: change the site or the object layout and the result changes. RoboColosseum tests five robot foundation models and three frontier LLM agents head to head on four robot types at many real sites, with both models facing the same local conditions. Frontier agents match models specialized for robots, but every system struggles to finish open-world tasks reliably. Success alone hides differences: on the G1 humanoid no policy completed any task, yet each task has several preset completion conditions and progress is the share met, and average progress still ranged from 13.3% to 23.2%. ==Rankings agree only weakly across different robots==, so evaluation should span several robots and look at progress.

papers.title: Kimodo-Policy: Learning Kinematic Action Models for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.authors: Yunheng Wang, Jiaxi Zhang, Wei Lu, Yuetong Fang, Taowen Wang, Yixiao Feng, Shuning Zhang, Junzhe Xu, Yichi Wang, Zizhao ...
papers.summary: A humanoid that walks while picking things up needs whole-body coordination, yet current models mostly inherit semantic or video pretraining and still have to learn how the body moves downstream. This paper changes the pretraining target: it takes a model that generates whole-body motion from text, freezes it as the backbone, and trains only a small branch that feeds in camera images plus the hand control. With the same structure randomly initialized and then trained, success on object-interaction tasks falls from 51.67% to 18.33%. Across eight real-robot tasks it averages 60% success, while its lead on simulation leaderboards is small. ==With motion itself as the pretraining target, the downstream work is only connecting it to images==, much like freezing a pretrained model and training only an adapter layer in recommendation.

papers.title: Learn the Task, Not the Schedule: Reducing Spurious Cross-Arm Coupling in Bimanual Imitation Learning
papers.authors: Shuyuan Hu, Deng-Ke Wu, Yifan Jin, Qianhang Luo, Mingchen Ju, Kai Ye, Bo Zhao
papers.summary: In two-armed robot demonstrations, which hand moves first is often just the operator's habit, yet imitation learning turns it into a rule, so pausing one arm makes the other wait too. The authors cut each arm's recording into segments and retime them while keeping the necessary orderings, such as opening a drawer before putting something in, which creates many schedules with no new data collection. On a real robot, a 4-second pause of one arm costs the other arm 2.56 extra seconds for a policy trained only on concurrent starts, and just 0.25 seconds with the new method. When the drawer is closed, the policy stops and waits every time. ==Coincidences in demonstration order get learned as signals==, which anyone in recommendation will recognize from spurious correlations caused by exposure order.

papers.title: SimDuoReal: Object-Centric Bimanual Policy for Emergent Dexterity
papers.authors: Qiyang Yan, Yulin Liu, Akash Sharma, Haozhi Qi, Guanya Shi, C. Karen Liu
papers.summary: Getting two dexterous hands to cooperate has usually meant writing a separate reward for each behavior, spelling out which hand moves and when to hand over. This paper uses one reward that only checks whether the object reached its goal pose, and changes the training environments instead, for example by placing the goal in the other hand's workspace so the object must be passed across. Grasping, in-hand adjustment and handover all appear in the trained policies. After three expert policies are distilled into one, it succeeds 76.3% of the time on real hardware across four tasks with unseen objects and no task-specific fine-tuning. In simulated barcode scanning it reaches 85.0%, while two single-arm policies without handover reach 60.4%. ==The engineering effort moves from writing rewards to designing the training distribution==, the same trade-off recommendation engineers face when tuning sample distributions.

papers.title: Tactile Sensors Are an Effective Substitute for Wrist Cameras in Contact-Rich or Occluded Manipulation
papers.authors: Aijia Yang, Arsh Tangri, Sergey Zakharov, Krishna Murthy Jatavallabhula
papers.summary: Wrist cameras are almost standard on robot-arm policies, yet once the fingers close, the actual contact is hidden from them too. The authors attach two low-cost tactile arrays inside the gripper and feed the readings as two extra images into the same ACT policy, with demonstrations and training settings unchanged. On retrieving an item from an opaque bag, inserting a plug and wiping a whiteboard, the policy with touch and no wrist camera beats the vision-only policy with a wrist camera every time, significantly so on two tasks, with 81.7% against 50.0% on retrieval. Adding both does not reliably help. ==Signals worth adding are the ones that do not overlap existing inputs==, which also holds when adding features to a ranking model.

papers.title: Compass 1: Towards Open-World and Persistent Embodied Navigation from Monocular RGB Videos
papers.authors: Hai Zhang, Siqi Liang, Yanjun Guo, Shoufeng Zhang, Yunhao Wang, Hangyu Du, Haoguang Mai, Hongchen Li, Jiazhi Yang, Jialo...
papers.summary: Navigation models usually can use only the last few frames, so returning to a target that went out of sight long ago is close to impossible. Compass 1 draws its past trajectory as a 2D map labeled with keyframe indices and headings, and feeds it with sparse keyframes as ordinary images, leaving the model architecture unchanged. The map alone does nothing because the model ignores it, so training adds question-answering supervision on which frame shows the target and which direction to go now. Overall real-world success is 79.4%, against 17.8% for the strongest baseline. On returning to an out-of-sight target every baseline fails, while Compass 1 reaches 58%. ==History has to be compressed, and supervision has to force the model to use it==, which is also the sticking point in long-term behavior sequence modeling.

papers.title: Meituan-Robotics-0: A Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Desktop Manipulation
papers.authors: Meituan Robotics Team, Caicheng Wang, Chen Zhao, Chengpeng Jin, Duo Xu, Fengjiao Chen, Guanglu Wan, Heqing Yang, Jia Wan...
papers.summary: General desktop manipulation has to learn a behavior prior from messy data, transfer across robot bodies, recover after a closed-loop mistake, and keep task state for longer. This work turns large vision-language collections and robot trajectories that cover twelve embodiments into executable control in three stages. It first pretrains the backbone with discrete action tokens. It then replaces the discrete head with a continuous action head initialized from scratch and uses flow matching on unified end-effector action chunks for cross-embodiment control. Finally it post-trains on the real robot with successful demonstrations, corrections in which a person first decides whether to take over and then supplies the right motion, and autonomous rollouts labeled by outcome. As a standalone policy it reaches 93.6% success on RoboTwin 2.0. Data collection rolls back the segment where the policy failed and lets a person attach the correct motion; after training on those corrections, Ethernet-insertion success reaches 70%.

papers.title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
papers.authors: Chen Chen, Omid Bagherieh, Naveen Nikamanth Appiah Balaji, Jesse T. Gonzalez, Negin Heravi, Fahad Islam, Xueting Li, Jea...
papers.summary: Robot manipulation does not have to rely on specialist policies trained on large sets of demonstrations. In this paper a generalist AI model acts as an agent, commands the robot arm directly and adjusts as the task unfolds, with no demonstrations and no task-specific training, and it succeeds far more often than specially trained VLA policies. The authors' reference harness, AMP1, reaches an 85.6% zero-shot success rate on the RoboLab-120 benchmark, against 49.2% for the leading VLA policy, and it succeeds in nearly all real-robot trials across three robots and twelve tasks. The harness supplies no grasping, pushing or placing skills, so the agent works out its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools and calibrating its cameras. A generalist model used directly as the controller may be more general and more robust than a specially trained policy.

papers.title: Gemini Robotics 2.5 accelerates real-world general dexterity
papers.summary: DeepMind has released Gemini Robotics 2.5 and calls it its most capable vision-language-action model, a kind of model that takes in images and text instructions and outputs robot actions directly. The upgrade is pitched on dexterity, reliability and safety, and the title stresses general dexterity in the real world. Putting reliability and safety among the headline claims reflects the same concern as not judging a production system by offline metrics alone.
